title: A cyclic-colormap angle field: how does phase or direction vary?
summary: A quantity that is an angle, such as the argument of a complex function, wraps around: just after pi comes minus pi. A cyclic colour map makes the colour seam disappear, so singular points show as places where all colours meet.

media.alt: A square plot coloured with a cyclic orange, purple and blue-white palette. Orange circles mark two zeros, an orange square marks one pole, all at points where every colour meets. A small ring-shaped colour wheel at the upper right labels the angles 0, pi/2, pi and minus pi/2.
media.caption: Reference render of class F2.5 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: How does phase or direction vary?
read_the_figure.axes: x and y: the complex plane, equal scale, -2 to 2. Colour: arg w(z), the angle of w = (z^2 - 1)/(z - 0.5 - 0.5i), from -pi to pi on a cyclic palette. The inset colour wheel is the key: 0 at the right, pi/2 at the top, pi at the left, -pi/2 at the bottom.
look_at: Find the points where all colours meet. What is at each: a zero or a pole?
Walk counter-clockwise around one of them: do the colours go through the wheel once, and in which order?
Is there a visible seam where the angle jumps from pi to -pi? With a cyclic map there should be none.
Compare the order of colours around the square marker with that around the circles.
as_drawn: Two zeros, z = 1 and z = -1 (circles), and one pole, z = 0.5 + 0.5i (square), are marked in amber.
The winding number, computed numerically on small circles, is +1 around each zero and -1 around the pole; on |z| = 2 it is +1 (two zeros minus one pole).
The colour wheel gives the key as required; the figure shows phase only. The magnitude |w| is not drawn, so zeros and poles look alike apart from the colour order.
read_the_figure.proves: Where the phase is undefined and how many times it winds around each point. It cannot tell a zero from a pole by itself without the direction of the colour cycle or an extra magnitude layer.
if_wrong: A non-cyclic colour map (viridis or a rainbow with a hard end): a false edge at plus and minus pi.
No colour wheel: colours cannot be turned into angles.
A cyclic map with strong lightness changes: the eye reads brightness as magnitude.

terms.meaning: The angle of a complex number measured from the positive real axis.
A colour map whose two ends are the same colour, so angle plus or minus pi has no seam.
A point where w = 0. The phase winds once counter-clockwise around a simple zero.
A point where w is infinite. The phase winds once clockwise around a simple pole.
The net number of turns the phase makes along a closed path.
A key that shows which colour means which angle.

remember: Angle needs a cyclic colour map.
Colour order around a point: counter-clockwise = zero, clockwise = pole (counting simple ones).
Always include a colour wheel with angles labelled.
Winding number = zeros - poles inside the path.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position is the complex plane. Colour is a single number, the angle, mapped on a cycle so that the left and right ends match. The inset wheel is the legend. Amber open markers are analysis overlays at the zeros and the pole.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A phase is a point on a circle, not a number on a line, so a line-shaped colour bar is the wrong key: it implies that pi is far from -pi. A cyclic colour map closes the circle. The result shows that the phase varies smoothly everywhere except at zeros and poles, where it takes every value in an arbitrarily small neighbourhood.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A map that is not cyclic or not uniform in lightness produces false edges or false maxima. Colours alone hide the magnitude, so a near zero and a near pole look similar. The eye also tends to read lightness as value; some cyclic maps vary strongly in lightness. And on a coarse image the points where colours meet are tiny and easy to miss.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: The colour wheel is the only way to read an angle from a colour. A cyclic-only map makes sure the picture has no artificial boundary. Without them the figure is decoration.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Domain colouring adds brightness for the magnitude, which separates zeros from poles at a glance. Contours of constant phase lines are a plain-line alternative. For director fields (angles modulo pi) use short line segments. For spin or orientation data use a cyclic map or glyphs.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add brightness bands for log |w| so zeros darken and poles brighten, and print the winding number next to each marked point.

steps.title: Winding number and the argument principle
steps.note: Z and P count zeros and poles inside C. Computed on small circles: +1 around z = 1, +1 around z = -1, -1 around z = 0.5 + 0.5i; on the circle |z| = 2: 2 - 1 = +1.

steps.title: Why a zero looks like a colour wheel
steps.note: Near a simple zero the phase equals the angle around the point plus a constant, so the colours reproduce the wheel. Near a pole w behaves like 1/(z - p), whose argument is minus the angle: the colours run the other way.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) how many points have all colours meeting and what are they? (2) In which direction do the colours cycle around the square? (3) What is the net winding on a large circle?

solution.text: Three: z = -1 and z = 1 (circles) and 0.5 + 0.5i (square). From the formula the numerator z^2 - 1 vanishes at plus and minus 1 and the denominator at 0.5 + 0.5i.
Opposite to the circles: the circles are zeros (colours go round counter-clockwise) and the square is a pole (clockwise).
Two zeros minus one pole: +1. Around the edge of the plot the colours go once round the wheel.

worked.answer: Three special points (two zeros, one pole), opposite cycle directions for zero and pole, and net winding +1 on a large circle.

checks.q: Why must an angle be plotted with a cyclic colour map?
checks.answer: Because angles wrap: plus pi and minus pi are the same direction. A cyclic map makes them the same colour, so no false seam appears.

checks.q: The phase winds once counter-clockwise around a point. Is it a zero or a pole?
checks.answer: A simple zero. A simple pole winds clockwise.

checks.q: A phase map shows three meeting points. What extra information would you need to say which are zeros?
checks.answer: The cycle direction around each (counter-clockwise = zero) or a second layer showing log of the magnitude.
